title: Proof Pile
user: People with multi-drive photo libraries who need to remove duplicates and low-value shots without accidentally deleting the only meaningful copy.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A 2 TB library owner says duplicates and unwanted media are making backup cost and browsing unusable, and asks for practical removal strategies.
A separate user with tens of thousands of phone photos wants local duplicate detection and repair of incorrect EXIF ordering, explicitly avoiding uploads to a random site.

recurrence: Two independent 2025 Ask HN requests, each describing tens of thousands to terabytes of media; a wrong deletion is irreversible and makes batch cleanup frightening.
current_workaround: Use Photos/Google Photos, run dupeGuru or PhotoSweeper, then manually inspect folders and keep excess copies rather than risk a deletion.
incumbents_and_gap: dupeGuru, Gemini 2, PhotoSweeper, and Immich identify similar files, but do not make a portable evidence-backed deletion decision (all copies, metadata differences, related burst) the primary artifact.
smallest_useful_product: Local desktop/PWA scanner that groups exact, perceptual, and metadata-near duplicates; shows every copy's path, dimensions, EXIF and backup presence; then writes an undoable move-to-quarantine plan and CSV decision log. Non-goals: cloud photo hosting, face recognition, or auto-deletion.
success_measure: In a 30-day pilot, 70% of users complete a reviewed quarantine of at least 500 files and restore fewer than 1% of chosen files.
monetization: one-time — sensitive local media cleanup needs a trustworthy purchase, not an ongoing account.
constraints: Process images locally; never transmit thumbnails by default; preserve originals and metadata; use OS trash/quarantine rather than permanent delete; clearly warn that backup parity is not a substitute for restore testing.
why_distinct: The product is a defensible review-and-reversal workflow for cleanup, not another gallery or magic duplicate detector.

title: Family Photo Ledger
user: A family member inheriting scans, negatives, phones, and cloud exports who must build a shareable archive without losing provenance, ownership, or who received which copy.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A user has 4,729 digitized family slides spanning the 1960s–2000s, with partial labels and broken chronology, and asks for a safe preservation flow.
After a relative died, a family member needs to scan prints/negatives and gather high-quality digital copies across a complex family, asking what works for an archive everyone can access.

recurrence: Two separate 2026 family-archive requests; the job commonly arrives after a death, when provenance and sharing decisions are emotionally and practically high stakes.
current_workaround: Put scans in Drive, Google Photos, Dropbox, or a shared hard drive; rename files manually and communicate ownership in email threads.
incumbents_and_gap: Google Photos, Immich, Lightroom, and Mylio organize media, but do not produce a handoff ledger covering source medium, scan status, rights/contact notes, and delivery to family branches.
smallest_useful_product: Offline-first archive manifest maker: import folders, assign source/custodian/date-confidence notes, create a family-safe share package with contact sheet and checksums, and export an editable CSV/JSON ledger. Non-goals: image hosting, facial identification, genealogy database, or AI restoration.
success_measure: At least 60% of pilot archives export a manifest plus two recipient packages, with every delivered asset traceable to a source folder or physical item ID.
monetization: one-time — archive projects are episodic and families need files that remain usable without a subscription.
constraints: No automatic public sharing; local-only by default; state clearly that copyright/privacy permissions are the archivist's responsibility; preserve original checksums and never alter masters.
why_distinct: It is a provenance and handoff utility around an archive, not a competing photo library.

title: File Home Map
user: People overwhelmed by years of documents and downloads who need a low-pressure way to decide where files belong and make progress without a risky mass reorganization.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A user describes spending countless minutes deciding directory names and locations for code and PDFs, then being unable to remember where anything belongs.
A partner's digital hoard spans mailboxes, drives, folders, cloud storage and notes, with similar/duplicate content ungrouped by project or subject.

recurrence: Two independent requests across 2025–2026 describe the same decision paralysis across many storage locations; the severity is chronic avoidance rather than a one-time tidy-up.
current_workaround: Create another top-level folder, search by filename, use Finder/Explorer tags, or attempt a weekend move that is abandoned midway.
incumbents_and_gap: Finder/Explorer, Hazel, TagSpaces, and Everything help navigate or automate rules, but they do not provide a reversible, human-paced queue for deciding a file's home across an existing mess.
smallest_useful_product: A local desktop queue that inventories selected folders, clusters likely project/duplicate items without moving them, lets a user define a small destination map, and generates an undoable move plan plus a 'decide later' inbox. Non-goals: AI auto-filing, cloud sync, email ingestion, or replacing the filesystem.
success_measure: Half of pilots clear or intentionally defer 1,000 inventory items in four sessions, while fewer than 2% of planned moves are undone.
monetization: one-time — the utility operates on a personal backlog and has no justified recurring service cost.
constraints: Index filenames and metadata locally; never make moves until explicit confirmation; support dry-run and rollback journals; avoid claims that inferred clusters are correct.
why_distinct: It helps users establish a durable decision system before changing their files, rather than offering another automatic organizer.

title: Export Receipt
user: People leaving or backing up online services who need to know whether an export is complete, intelligible, and reusable before they lose access.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A user asks why there is no comprehensive local tool for exporting/transferring personal data across services, noting that exercising portability rights is impractical.
A separate user reports a ChatGPT export request still has not arrived after 30 days and highlights the legal and practical importance of accessing personal data.

recurrence: Two explicit data-portability requests in consecutive years; the harm is lock-in or silent data loss at exactly the time a user is changing providers.
current_workaround: Request a ZIP, inspect a few files manually, store it unopened, or write a bespoke parser for a single service.
incumbents_and_gap: Google Takeout, Apple Data & Privacy, and vendor-specific exports create archives; Data Transfer Project targets provider integrations. Neither gives end users a local, vendor-agnostic receipt saying what is present, missing, unreadable, or not yet portable.
smallest_useful_product: A local web app with pluggable archive inspectors for common ZIP/JSON/CSV exports; it inventories counts, attachments, date ranges, parse errors, hashes, and creates a signed HTML/JSON receipt with a retest checklist. Non-goals: credential login, scraping, automatic account migration, or hosted storage.
success_measure: For supported exports, 90% of pilot users can identify the archive's date coverage and at least one missing/ambiguous category in under five minutes.
monetization: free — open local inspection builds trust and adoption; paid support for organizational export formats can follow.
constraints: All parsing must happen in-browser; archives can contain hostile paths/content; do not make legal-compliance promises; plugin parsers need clear licenses and fixtures without private data.
why_distinct: It verifies an export rather than promising impossible universal extraction or becoming another cloud backup product.

title: Family Paper Vault
user: A household coordinator who needs to hand off searchable scans, notes, and important records to relatives without granting everyone unrestricted access to a cloud drive.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A user asks how to organize and share family documents, tax scans, notes/to-do lists, and photos in one workable arrangement.
A multilingual user scans invoices, medical papers, and government documents and needs search even when they cannot remember the document's language.

recurrence: Two late-2025 requests show a repeated household handoff problem: records are both sensitive and hard to find, especially across languages.
current_workaround: Use a shared Drive/Dropbox folder, send attachments in chat, or maintain personal scans in a document app no relative can navigate.
incumbents_and_gap: Google Drive, Dropbox, Paperless-ngx, and DEVONthink store/search documents, but a simple exportable household packet with role-based bundles and an explicit handoff index is not their core workflow.
smallest_useful_product: A local-first packager that creates encrypted or plain recipient bundles from chosen documents, with a human-written index, expiry/review notes, optional local OCR text, and a print-ready recovery card. Non-goals: hosted document management, legal advice, medical-record portal, or automatic translation.
success_measure: In pilot households, each pack has a named recipient and recovery instructions, and a recipient finds a requested record in under two minutes without the organizer present.
monetization: one-time — families need durable files and clear ownership, not another long-lived data custodian.
constraints: Treat documents as highly sensitive; encrypt locally with user-controlled keys; do not transmit or train on OCR text; explain that packet recipients can copy unencrypted files after opening.
why_distinct: It creates a deliberate, survivable handoff artifact rather than a general document cloud.

title: Storage Exit Check
user: Privacy-conscious individuals moving files from cloud storage to a NAS or local disks who need evidence their replacement is complete and recoverable before cancelling a subscription.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A user considering moving away from cloud storage asks why others never moved, or moved back, reflecting uncertainty around the trade-offs.
A separate discussion proposes local and off-site NAS replication with rsync/TrueNAS and asks about the real cloud-versus-local trade-offs.

recurrence: Two independent 2025 discussions show that storage migration decisions hinge on trust in sync, replication, and recovery—not merely copying a folder once.
current_workaround: Run rsync/Syncthing/restic and compare free-space numbers, or retain cloud subscriptions indefinitely because no one has tested a restore.
incumbents_and_gap: rsync, Syncthing, restic, Duplicati, and NAS dashboards execute transfers, but a novice-readable exit checklist comparing source/destination manifests and proving a sampled restore is absent.
smallest_useful_product: A local CLI that snapshots two directory trees, explains count/size/hash differences, selects a reproducible restore sample, and emits a printable cancellation-ready report. Non-goals: backup daemon, cloud API credential manager, encryption service, or NAS administration.
success_measure: At least 75% of pilots complete a documented sampled restore before disabling a source sync or subscription; zero source deletions are initiated by the tool.
monetization: free — auditability is more credible as an inspectable local utility; paid setup help is possible later.
constraints: Read-only by default; hashes can be slow and expose filenames in reports, so support redaction; never imply a sample proves disaster recovery; document filesystem timestamp and symlink differences.
why_distinct: It is a migration confidence and restore-evidence layer, not another sync or backup engine.

title: Import Recipe
user: Operations and implementation staff who repeatedly clean a source spreadsheet into a vendor's rigid import template and need the transformation to be reviewable and reusable.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A practitioner asks how people handle date formatting, template alignment, and old-to-new code mapping before Salesforce, Workday, NetSuite, and other imports.
A separate request for CSV formulas is motivated by maintaining local personal databases that are more useful than plain CSV while remaining shareable text.

recurrence: Two independent import/CSV workflow discussions; this work is repetitive, error-prone, and often performed manually in spreadsheets under deadline.
current_workaround: Use Excel formulas, Power Query, copy/paste, one-off scripts, and an undocumented mapping workbook that breaks on the next import.
incumbents_and_gap: Excel/Power Query, OpenRefine, Dataiku, and enterprise ETL tools transform data, but small teams lack a tiny, shareable recipe that validates against a supplied template and produces a handoff diff.
smallest_useful_product: Offline browser tool: load CSV/XLSX source and a blank template, define column mappings/normalizers/lookups, preview rejects and row diffs, then save a portable JSON recipe and output CSV. Non-goals: SaaS connectors, scheduled pipelines, database writes, or AI column guessing.
success_measure: A user reruns a saved recipe on a second monthly file with no formula edits and reduces rejected rows by at least 50% versus their baseline.
monetization: one-time — a local file transformer has value without data hosting or per-seat lock-in.
constraints: Files remain in-browser; cap memory/use streaming where possible; workbook formula evaluation must be explicit; mappings may contain personal data and should not be sent to telemetry.
why_distinct: It productizes the reviewed mapping recipe and exceptions handoff, rather than competing as a broad ETL platform.

title: Workbook Constellation
user: People inheriting operational or financial workbooks who need to see cross-tab formula dependencies before changing a cell or handing the workbook to another owner.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A user with dozens of spreadsheet tabs says built-in tracing is one-cell-at-a-time and asks for a big-picture cross-tab dependency map.
A marketing professional reports paid AI tools miss spreadsheet data or draw incorrect conclusions, making reliable structural understanding more urgent.

recurrence: Two 2025 spreadsheet requests point to costly interpretation failures: dependency discovery can take hours and AI summaries cannot be trusted as the verification step.
current_workaround: Click Excel/Sheets trace precedents one cell at a time, build a manual tab map, buy an enterprise add-in, or ask an AI and manually verify it.
incumbents_and_gap: Excel trace tools, Google Sheets formula view, and specialist auditors exist, but lightweight cross-platform, read-only maps for a specific workbook handoff remain awkward and expensive.
smallest_useful_product: A local XLSX parser that extracts formulas, generates a navigable tab-to-tab dependency graph, flags external links/circular references/opaque formulas, and exports a static handoff report. Non-goals: spreadsheet editing, calculation engine, macro execution, or AI analysis.
success_measure: In a pilot, a new workbook owner identifies the upstream source of five sampled output cells in under ten minutes, with the report matching manual inspection at least 95% of the time.
monetization: one-time — workbook audits are episodic and users should not upload business files for a recurring fee.
constraints: Parse untrusted XLSX defensively; never execute macros or external links; keep workbooks local; document unsupported formula dialects and protected/encrypted-file limitations.
why_distinct: It offers structural proof for human review, not an opaque AI spreadsheet analyst or another spreadsheet editor.

title: Vendor Billing Inbox
user: A small-business operator who needs every SaaS invoice collected and matchable without logging into dozens of billing portals at month-end.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A user says SaaS vendors including OpenAI and Cursor force monthly portal logins to download invoices and asks why invoices cannot simply arrive by email.
A separate Ask HN post asks why invoice matching is still painful in 2026, showing the collection problem continues into reconciliation.

recurrence: Two distinct finance-operations requests in 2025–2026; missed invoices create close delays, duplicate payment risk, and tax-record gaps.
current_workaround: Log into each portal, forward PDFs to an accountant, use a generic receipt app, or wait for the bookkeeper to report a missing charge.
incumbents_and_gap: Dext, Hubdoc, Expensify, QuickBooks, and Xero ingest documents, but they are accounting suites or paid capture services rather than a small vendor-portal obligation register with a clear missing-invoice chase list.
smallest_useful_product: A privacy-first inbox/desktop app that accepts forwarded invoice emails and PDFs, records vendor-period-amount, deduplicates files, matches a supplied card CSV, and produces a 'missing invoice' checklist. Non-goals: portal scraping, payment initiation, tax advice, or bookkeeping ledger replacement.
success_measure: A five-vendor pilot closes a month with 95% of card charges either matched to an invoice or explicitly listed for follow-up within 15 minutes.
monetization: one-time — individual operators want a narrow utility before committing to a complete accounting product.
constraints: Invoices contain financial and personal data; default to local storage/encryption; preserve original files; OCR confidence must be reviewable; never impersonate users or bypass portal controls.
why_distinct: It resolves the gap between billing portals and accounting software: knowing exactly which proof document is missing.

title: Invoice Handoff Sheet
user: Freelancers and small agencies who need a clear, non-confrontational record of what was delivered, invoiced, due, and followed up before a client payment becomes a dispute.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A freelancer describes repeatedly being ghosted after completed work and invoices, then manually chasing payment while refreshing Stripe.
A separate invoicing discussion recommends a single clearly structured page with milestone dates, amounts, project total, and the next amount due.

recurrence: Two independent freelancer-oriented discussions show that invoicing failure is often a missing shared status record, not merely an inability to generate a PDF.
current_workaround: Send an invoice PDF and follow-up emails, track milestones in a separate project tool, and manually reconstruct what the client received when payment is late.
incumbents_and_gap: Stripe Invoicing, FreshBooks, Wave, and QuickBooks send invoices and reminders, but do not make a tiny client-shareable delivery-to-payment handoff timeline that works even when the client will not adopt a portal.
smallest_useful_product: A static-web generator for a signed project handoff page: milestones, acceptance links/files, invoice identifier, due date, payment instructions, and an exportable follow-up log. Non-goals: payment processing, automated collections, credit scoring, legal notices, or CRM.
success_measure: In pilot projects, 80% of invoices have a linked delivery/acceptance record and users spend less than five minutes preparing a first follow-up.
monetization: one-time — a template-oriented client handoff utility has transparent value with no need to retain payment data.
constraints: Do not claim legal enforceability; users control hosted files and personal data; support export; avoid dark-pattern reminders or automated escalating messages.
why_distinct: The core object is an auditable delivery-and-payment handoff, not another invoice generator or debt-collection bot.

title: Focus Lens
user: Knowledge workers with low vision who use browser-heavy enterprise apps and need predictable magnification, focus visibility, and keyboard orientation on sites that provide poor accessibility support.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A knowledge worker with progressively worsening vision says modern web apps such as PowerBI and Salesforce lack usable keybindings and asks what will support the transition.
A separate accessibility discussion notes that API-based assistive software fails on unsupported or remote software and asks what broader-help tools are actually usable.

recurrence: Two 2025 accessibility requests describe barriers across modern web and remote applications; failure blocks sustained professional work rather than a cosmetic preference.
current_workaround: Use OS magnification, browser zoom, screen readers, voice control, or ask an employer for accommodations; each breaks down on dense web UIs or inconsistent focus order.
incumbents_and_gap: Windows Magnifier, macOS Zoom, Chrome zoom, Reader Mode, and screen readers are essential, but do not offer a per-site visual focus rail and user-owned keyboard waypoint layer for arbitrary web-app workflows.
smallest_useful_product: A browser extension with large high-contrast focus indicator, temporary reading lane, per-site zoom/contrast presets, user-defined named focus waypoints, and an exportable shortcut cheat sheet. Non-goals: screen-reader replacement, computer-vision surveillance, AI interpretation, or bypassing site security.
success_measure: In a two-week usability pilot, participants complete three recurring browser workflows with 30% fewer lost-focus events than with browser zoom alone.
monetization: free — core accessibility assistance should be accessible; optional paid enterprise deployment/support must not restrict basic features.
constraints: Follow WCAG and browser extension permission minimization; all configuration stays local; do not capture page content; test with low-vision users before claiming benefit.
why_distinct: It improves orientation in hostile web apps through deterministic user controls, not an unreliable visual-AI assistant.

title: Bookmark Proofbook
user: People with thousands of browser bookmarks who need to retain why a link mattered and export a durable local collection as bookmarking services disappear.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A user notes that beloved bookmarking services such as Delicious and Pocket died and asks how saved links can still lead back to something worth revisiting.
A separate user with thousands of bookmarks says manual folders became unmanageable and asks for categorization plus search over the linked page content.

recurrence: Two independent 2025 requests combine service churn with unmanageable large bookmark collections; a URL alone loses context and eventually rots.
current_workaround: Keep browser folders, move to Raindrop/Pinboard, use Pocket until it closes, or rely on browser history/search and never clean the collection.
incumbents_and_gap: Raindrop.io, Pinboard, Linkwarden, Wallabag, and browser bookmarks store links, but a no-account portable 'reason plus evidence' capture with periodic local export and link-change report is still a narrow gap.
smallest_useful_product: Browser extension that captures a bookmark with user-written reason, title, selected text and content hash; imports browser HTML, offers local full-text search, and exports a self-contained HTML/JSON proofbook with link-health changes. Non-goals: social bookmarking, cloud sync, automatic LLM summaries, or web-page piracy.
success_measure: Within 30 days, 50% of pilots import 500+ links and successfully retrieve five previously forgotten resources by their own saved context.
monetization: one-time — durable personal archives should not depend on an account surviving another service shutdown.
constraints: Require explicit capture action; respect page permissions and do not bypass paywalls; limit stored page extracts; ensure exports are user-controlled and portable.
why_distinct: It treats a bookmark as a portable research assertion with provenance, not another feed, read-later app, or LLM tagging wrapper.
